tip: Write an array on paper and trace each index while you read the code.
Write one sentence saying what the function returns, then test it with two inputs.
Make a small table of each variable name and its value after every line.
List each condition and write down which branch runs for one true and one false case.
Print each character with its index to see how slicing works.
Write three key and value pairs, then look up each key by hand.
Do the same step to both sides and check the answer by substituting it back.
Convert the percentage to a fraction first, then multiply by the total.
Sketch the shape and label every angle you know before solving for the missing one.
Draw a truth table for the gate and test each input pair.
Write the place values 128, 64, 32 and so on above each bit and add the ones that are set.
Open a small text file, read one line, print it and close the file.
Add a print statement before the failing line to see the value that causes the error.
Describe one real object, list its properties and actions, then write them as a class.
Trigger the error on purpose, read the message and wrap that line in try and except.
Draw each vector as an arrow from the origin and add them tip to tail.
Sort the numbers first, then find the middle value and compare it with the average.
List all orders of three items by hand before using the formula.
Write every true and false combination in rows and fill one column at a time.
Draw a box for each variable and an arrow to the box it points to.
Write the counter value after each pass so you can see when the loop stops.
Draw a parent class box with an arrow to each child and list what the child adds.
Sketch one table with three columns and write two sample rows before querying it.
Number the nodes in the order you visit them while tracing the search on a drawing.
Fill a small table by hand and note which earlier cells each new cell uses.
Count the choices for a tiny case such as two of four items before using a formula.
Convert one small number between decimal and binary by hand and check it back.
Write the first five terms and look for what changes between neighbors.
Draw a tree with one branch per outcome and multiply along each path.
Draw a box for each process and mark which one holds the CPU at each time step.
